talks.teaser: Expo West 2024: BUILDING HEALTHY AND HIGH-PERFORMING TECH TEAMS PANEL.
talks.summary:
Overview: A panel at Expo West discusses building healthy, high-performing technology teams, exploring leadership challenges in diverse, distributed engineering organizations across global technology companies.

Key Topics: Balancing productivity with team wellbeing; cross-cultural communication challenges referenced via Erin Meyer's Culture Map framework; managing diverse team expectations across time zones; and harmonizing competing business requirements with employee needs.

Technical Details: Panelists from Amazon and other technology organizations share experiences managing globally distributed teams with varying cultural communication styles. They emphasize that leadership success depends on communication quality and cultural awareness across boundaries.

Takeaways: High-performing tech teams require intentional culture-building and cross-cultural communication skills. Leaders must understand how cultural backgrounds shape team dynamics, expectations, and productivity patterns.

talks.title: Expo West 2024: BATTLING THROUGH BAD DATA: HOW TO SUCCEED IN AI
talks.teaser: Expo West 2024: BATTLING THROUGH BAD DATA: HOW TO SUCCEED IN AI.
talks.summary:
Why AI Projects Fail

Dr Janet Bastman, Napier AI chief data scientist, opens with a rhetorical question about money wasted on doomed AI efforts. She cites Memorial Sloan Kettering’s IBM Watson cancer project—launched with fanfare, scrapped by 2018 after doctors called recommendations unsafe, costing about $62 million over six years as a cautionary example.

Rejecting Magic-Box Thinking

Bastman contrasts vendor hype—gather data, feed AI, get answers—with data science discipline. She argues science is magic that works, and that niche medical summarization remains hard even for modern LLMs. Failed projects often skip user feedback, doctor validation, and iterative checks.

Defining and Fixing Bad Data

Bad data means information unfit for purpose: inconsistent, unbalanced, inaccurate, or unrepresentative samples that mislead models. Bastman urges applying scientific principles—clear problem definition, representative sampling, and honest assessment of whether datasets support confident answers—before scaling investment.

talks.title: Expo West 2024: HOW THE INTELLIGENCE REVOLUTION CAN DRIVE SOCIO-ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT
talks.teaser: Expo West 2024: HOW THE INTELLIGENCE REVOLUTION CAN DRIVE SOCIO-ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT.
talks.summary:
Planetary Stakes

NVIDIA senior scientist Allison Bishop opens with Rockström’s nine planetary boundaries, noting two-thirds are already breached. She ties climate harm to geopolitical oil dependence and argues visualization helps non-experts grasp risks and fund resilience.

Climate Visualization for Vulnerable Nations

At COP28 NVIDIA supported BOSS (Big Ocean Sustainable States) nations facing sea-level rise. Partners like RSS-Hydro use GPU tools to render physically accurate 3D scenarios—e.g., Tonga inundation by 2150—from elevation models, making abstract pledges tangible for policymakers.

Digital Twins and Mission-Critical AI

Examples include Cesium/Maxar digital twins of Cape Canaveral synced with live telemetry for launch safety, AV training in Omniverse metaverse environments, and Earth-2 climate/weather simulation. AI emulates physics to cut compute orders of magnitude while serving billion-user decision platforms.

Efficiency and Accessible Forecasting

NVIDIA highlights Green500 leadership and UK Isambard 3 Grace-Hopper systems. Models like CorrDiff downscale coarse climate data cheaply; ForecastNet demos show eight-line Python weather inference. Bishop credits gaming-driven GPU evolution now applied to humanitarian and planetary stewardship.

talks.title: Expo West 2024: EMBRACING TRANSFORMATIONAL LEADERSHIP
talks.teaser: Expo West 2024: EMBRACING TRANSFORMATIONAL LEADERSHIP.
talks.summary:
Leadership transformation

Ir Thompson John, JP Morgan Chase equities technology transformation executive, uses Satya Nadella's experience raising a son with cerebral palsy to illustrate how personal adversity can reshape corporate empathy, accessibility investment, and inclusive hiring at Microsoft after 2014.

From command to purpose

She contrasts command-and-control management with transformational leadership: emotional intelligence, feedback-seeking, purpose beyond bottom line, paid parental leave expansion, psychological safety to fail fast, and diversity of thinking as an innovation driver supported by research.

Collective intelligence

Drawing on agile mindset rather than tools alone, she advocates collective estimation, continuous collaboration, and tapping human plus machine intelligence across a two-thousand-person global organization. Leaders, she argues, can influence society beyond the firm by embedding CSR values such as those emphasized during Chase UK rollout.

talks.title: Expo West 2024: THE KEY TRENDS SHAPING THE FUTURE OF INFRASTRUCTURE
talks.teaser: Expo West 2024: THE KEY TRENDS SHAPING THE FUTURE OF INFRASTRUCTURE.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Arm's Cheryl Hung surveys infrastructure trends at Digit Expo West—from cloud-native maturity to AI engineering.

## Cloud-Native Divide
CNCF survey data shows beginners struggle with training and expertise, while mature cloud-native shops report security and complexity as top challenges—tooling proliferation hasn't simplified operations.

## Cloud-Native AI
Hung describes leveraging datacenter CPU/GPU capacity for AI workloads and the emergence of dedicated ML/AI engineer roles blending data science with infrastructure skills.

## Recommendations
She urges education so users understand AI they consume, and participation in communities like Linux Foundation AI/data and CNCF groups to track fast-moving standards.

## Takeaways
Infrastructure's next decade pairs cloud-native operations with AI scale—security and skills gaps remain the binding constraints.

talks.title: Scot-Secure 2024 | Session 1
talks.teaser: Three practitioners cover incident response planning, AI-driven endpoint prevention and threat hunting for security teams.
talks.summary:
Sonia Kumar, a global head of cyber defense, opens with lessons from responding to severe cyber attacks. She urges organisations to write an incident response plan before any incident, covering a severity risk matrix, communications routes and legal review. Her case study involved a high-privilege account nobody recognised, repeated shutdown requests against order-processing software, and a site-to-site VPN a supplier had set up years earlier and never removed after its contract ended. She advises against engaging extortionists, bringing in negotiators early, running board tabletop exercises and putting formal on-call arrangements in place.

Andy Bran, a sales engineer from BlackBerry, argues that signature-based antivirus leaves organisations exposed to new and polymorphic malware. He describes machine-learning models that judge a file from its static attributes, without signatures or execution, and cites results from a third-party test and a 2023 sample that an older model still blocked.

Melissa Goldsmith, a threat hunter, frames hunting around the assumption that compromise has already happened and the value of finding intruders early in the attack lifecycle. She suggests starting with narrow hunts such as process hierarchy, scripts making outbound connections, cloud version disabling and new user creation, filtering known-good activity as she goes. She stresses documentation, clear escalation paths to the SOC, and measuring success through escalations, new detections and ATT&CK coverage.

talks.title: ITSX Summit 2024 | Breakout E
talks.teaser: Coverage of ITSX Summit 2024 | Breakout E from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At the ITSX Summit 2024 Breakout E session, Asim Jalil, Sales Manager at EZO, delivered a presentation on improving employee experience and operational efficiency using self-service workflows and IT Asset Management (ITAM). Representing EZO—a US-based organization operating globally with products tracking over 75 million assets across more than 3,500 customers—Jalil explained how an employee-centric approach to IT Service Management (ITSM) enhances productivity, retention, and business growth. The session covered the core value of service catalogs, detailed features of EZO's ITAM platform 'AssetSonar', and addressed audience questions concerning lifecycle tracking, CMDB integration, and service desk interactions.

### Key Topics
- **Employee Experience & ITSM:** Emphasizing that employees are critical organizational assets, Jalil cited research indicating that positively engaged employees are over 16 times more engaged than dissatisfied counterparts. Common IT hurdles include delays at the service desk, incident handling bottlenecks, and a lack of self-service options.
- **Service Catalog Capabilities:** A structured service catalog offers targeted value propositions across roles: convenience and self-service for employees, streamlined request processing and context for help desk agents, and reduced SLA times, maintenance costs, and better procurement data for administrators.
- **Operational Scenarios:**
  1. *Onboarding:* Department-specific checklists enable automated or standardized requests (e.g., configuring Active Directory, assigning hardware, and provisioning software licenses).
  2. *Incident & Break-Fix Management:* If an employee damages hardware (e.g., a broken screen), they can log a ticket referencing their custody-assigned asset directly from the catalog or mobile app, immediately granting agents visibility into purchase dates, vendors, and linked software.
  3. *Software Access Requests:* Structured catalog workflows allow users to request specific applications (e.g., Zoho) without back-and-forth ambiguity.

### Technical Details
- **AssetSonar Core Features:** Serves as a single source of truth for hardware and software assets across hybrid, cloud, and on-premises environments. It includes an installed local agent, a centralized dashboard, auditing, alert management, and automated 24-hour synchronization.
- **Integrations & Hardware Management:** Integrates with discovery and endpoint platforms including Microsoft Intune, Jamf, SCCM, Meraki, and JumpCloud. It also connects with Dell for automated warranty synchronization and offers open APIs for enterprise systems like SAP.
- **Full Asset Lifecycle & Procurement:** Manages assets from procurement order generation to retirement. A dedicated purchase order module tracks vendor information, calculates automated depreciation, issues replacement alerts, and tracks refurbishment or disposal.
- **Upcoming Roadmap:** Planned features for AssetSonar and related EZO products include automated workflow-based triggers, a dedicated request portal, predictive analytics for vendor hardware reliability, configuration management database (CMDB) dependency mapping and anomaly detection, and generative AI/machine learning for catalog optimization and ticket analysis.

### Takeaways
During the Q&A segment, attendees pressed on how to track asset lifecycles across enterprise ERPs (like SAP), how CMDB functionality is handled, and how organizations should measure employee experience or discover user desires regarding chatbots and service desks. Jalil highlighted mobile application support for broken devices, planned SAP integrations, and noted that reducing resolution turnaround (e.g., cutting a multi-day delay down to same-day resolution) directly translates to improved employee satisfaction and reduced organizational friction.

talks.title: ITSX Summit 2024 | Session 1
talks.teaser: Covers service delivery leadership, new ways of working, and applying AI to service design, with ethics and governance in view.
talks.summary:
The session opens with three talks on running IT service and support teams. Alex Canter, director of technology at modular, argues that teams should stop tweaking processes that ought not to exist. He recommends measuring time taken and the risk and impact of errors to set priorities, and treating risk and audit as allies. In one change-management example, rethinking segregation of duties let engineers deploy directly, lifting deployments from about 900 over four years to 2,264 in the last year. His closing point is that policies only work when their intent is understood.

Ollie King, senior account executive at Halo itm, examines new ways of working. He traces how hybrid working was forced on workers during the pandemic and cites survey figures on people who would leave a role without it. He then describes the company's own practices: no fixed hierarchy, open workspaces, beta releases every two weeks and stable releases each quarter, unlimited annual leave, and a pledge against mergers or private equity deals for a rolling ten years. Brooks's law supports keeping teams lean.

Kate mcki, a senior service designer, explores applying AI across a design framework, from discovery through to measuring impact. She urges starting with small, managed pilots and bringing staff along. Her ethical concerns include bias in training data, manipulative personalisation, surveillance and synthetic misinformation, and she argues that transparency, governance and trust must be built alongside the technology.

talks.title: Fintech Summit 2023: Session 1
talks.teaser: Panellists weigh how regulation, embedded finance and legacy banks are reshaping fintech partnerships over the next decade.
talks.summary:
The opening session of this fintech summit in Scotland, its tenth, looked at how the sector has changed over the past decade and where it may head. Devi Mohan, who leads a fintech research firm, showed that regulation has grown heavier and changes far more often than before 2008. She expects partnerships, new data sources and the move from legacy systems to cloud to shape the next five years.

Fiona Henderson, a fintech specialist at CMS, explored embedded finance, where non-bank firms place lending and payments inside everyday customer journeys, often with bank funding behind them. Peter Crouch, chief information officer for business and commercial banking at Lloyds, described reshaping a 250-year-old bank into a leading fintech through five steps, from an innovation mindset and a technology overhaul to talent and partnerships. Andy Elfic of Barclays explained how the bank decides whether to build, buy or partner, and pointed to the fintech pledge and data-driven vetting for new suppliers.

The closing discussion covered cautious bank experiments with generative AI, the risks of reusing customer data, and the danger that branch closures leave older customers out. Panellists agreed that collaboration, simplifying legacy estates and changing culture matter most, while noting that many customers still keep their main account with a traditional bank.

talks.title: North Summit 2023 | Session 3
talks.teaser: Shows how linked, quality-checked data makes digital twins useful, then a panel weighs AI hype against real industrial use cases.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a talk from Charlotte McLean, engineering manager at a digital twin software company that runs a cloud workspace for collaboration. She argues that a 3D model on its own says little. Its value comes from linking it to equipment records, work orders, disciplines, hazards and documents pulled from customers' source systems. Her examples come from heavy asset industries such as oil and gas, where users can open a model and reach documents and process diagrams in one window. She stresses cross-checking incoming data, sending gap analyses back to customers, and being open about data quality. A side-by-side video comparison showed junction boxes placed differently in a model than in photogrammetry data.

Her closing takeaways were to understand what users need, to bring in only the data that is useful, and to build trust, since users blame the product when the data is poor. The panel that followed, with Ian Dugan, Luciano and nasima Brown, turned to AI and large language models. Panelists argued that AI is only as good as the data beneath it, and warned that generated answers can sound confident while being wrong. Nasima Brown described how her company adopted AI tools internally under a cautious policy on company data, while Ian Dugan urged organisations to prove value early in real use.

The discussion also covered regulation, with the EU AI Act and UK and Scottish initiatives raised as an enforcement gap for small firms. Panelists discussed the risk to entry-level jobs and how universities should teach critical thinking about AI output. The closing advice was to start with simple, practical use cases and to explain decisions to executives in plain business terms.

talks.title: North Summit 2023 | Session 1
talks.teaser: Executives share lessons on IT change, data-led transformation and securing business use of the metaverse.
talks.summary:
This morning session at a digital innovation summit in Aberdeen opened with Angus Murray reviewing a decade of IT and energy-sector change. He moved from server virtualization and collaboration tools to a service desk that resolved many issues on first contact, with first-time fix rates of 60 to 70 percent. He described a Windows 10 rollout that was reframed around staff benefits rather than security features, and then the energy transition, from large wind farms and a new gas plant to household batteries and off-peak tariffs. He closed with agile delivery teams and concern about automation and a just transition for workers.

Charlie Atkinson and Esther de Duran then walked through a business-led data transformation at INEOS, delivered with the consultancy Baringa. The team started from low data literacy, so they set value-linked KPIs, a governed data structure and training for business champions before building dashboards. The first wave was a daily operations report, followed by 28 reports and 105 automated pipelines, with a move away from Excel-based reporting. Lessons included avoiding dashboards built only by IT, setting boundaries on Excel, and choosing a partner who works alongside the client.

Rachel cool then looked at how businesses could operate safely in the metaverse, covering identity, privacy, digital asset theft and social engineering through avatars. She argued that established frameworks such as NIST still apply, while standards and regulation are still catching up. The session ended with a panel on skills and talent, where speakers stressed adoption over tool training, graduate programmes and keeping experienced staff involved.

talks.title: Leaders 2023: Session 2B
talks.teaser: Shows leaders how to push digital transformation through culture, short agile iterations and habits that make change stick.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a transformation director overseeing technology strategy across the portfolio companies of a private equity firm, starts with a background in physics and an early career that taught them to treat technology and the business as one. The core problem is that transformation demands investment and disruption up front, while rewards arrive only at the end, so many projects are abandoned during the dip. Changes are checked against three trends: agility and scale, whether something is a commodity or a differentiator, and automation and analytics, which rest on solid foundations.

Practical advice covers choosing technology at the right time, which often means fixing basics such as CRM, financial data and ERP, overcoming legacy thinking and bias, and building teams with new skills like user insight rather than traditional IT roles. On culture, the speaker argues it is set from the top and urges leaders to learn fast, measure outputs rather than inputs, encourage safe experimentation and give teams one thing to finish at a time. Agile is framed as a mindset for adapting to change, supported by short sprints and habits such as consistent meeting cadence, self-selected tasks and relative sizing with planning poker.

In the question session, an attendee asked how to handle people who think they practise scaled agile without understanding it. The answer was to explain the reasoning behind each practice and back it with real examples of success and failure. One case involved a director who expected a piece of work to take 12 weeks; a poker-based breakdown showed roughly a year and a half of work. The takeaway is that this kind of judgement builds through repetition.

talks.title: Leaders 2023: Session 2A
talks.teaser: Links burnout to stress and breathing habits, then guides the audience through a short nasal breathing exercise.
talks.summary:
John McPherson, who has spent about 25 years in mental health work and runs a well-being center, starts with his own story. After a severe breakdown in his twenties, he recovered through holistic practices, and he now sees people struggling with anxiety, depression and burnout. He describes burnout as a state where the body has lost its balance under constant pressure from poor sleep, diet, alcohol, worry and too much stimulation, and he argues that prevention matters more than long recovery.

The core of the talk is breathing. He explains that the nervous system has an activating side and a recovery side, and that slow nasal breathing supports recovery while mouth breathing keeps the body in a stress response. He describes taping the mouth shut at night, lengthening the exhale, and humming to stimulate the vagus nerve. He also mentions cold exposure, which he credits with easing his own chronic pain, and a young teacher with frequent panic attacks whom he says stopped having them after learning to breathe differently.

The session closes with a guided exercise lasting several minutes: nasal breathing with a short breath hold, attention moved through the body, and a moment spent recalling what it feels like to feel good. The practical takeaway is that a few minutes of intentional breathing each day can help people switch off stress before it builds into burnout.

talks.title: Leaders 2023: Session 2F
talks.teaser: Explains how isolating legacy applications in locked-down containers can help organisations pass the revised Cyber Essentials audit.
talks.summary:
The session explains how revised UK Cyber Essentials version 3 requirements, in force since late April, change audits for organisations running older software. Legacy systems once taken off the network must now be named in audit scope, and sandboxing or app-packaging tools no longer earn a pass when the application code still contains vulnerabilities.

The speaker presents an isolation layer that runs legacy and modern applications in containers. All inbound traffic is blocked except one encrypted port between client and server components, and outbound access is narrowed to what each application needs. Customer cases include a nuclear energy operator whose auditor, after a pen test, called anything inside a container an instant pass; a Royal Armories server migration finished in about 10 days; and a YMCA rollout across 40,000 seats on offline Linux tablets.

The presenter concedes the product's own code could need patching and that weak-password and multi-factor checks remain separate audit items. The takeaway is that containing a vulnerable application through tight inbound and outbound rules can keep it compliant without first fixing its code.

talks.title: Leaders 2023: Session 2C
talks.teaser: Argues that organisations should plan how a service will be retired from day one, using real cases of services that closed.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that products, services and prototypes almost always end, yet organisations rarely plan for it. Leaving things running is often the default because it seems cheaper. The speaker recalls a startup that only noticed forgotten prototypes when a cloud bill reached 70 000 pounds. Services close for many reasons, from temporary pandemic schemes and yearly charity funding to strategy shifts and sudden collapses such as Thomas Cook, which left 150 000 people abroad.

Hidden costs get particular attention. Customer data often must stay accessible for regulatory, analysis or fraud reasons, so retiring a service can mean building another one to serve data requests. Dependencies also cause trouble: when free school meals were opened to all primary pupils, the application data that had funded extra money for deprived schools dried up. Knowledge of how a system works can also leave with staff, which the speaker says is why some organisations create teams to keep service memory.

The advice is to ask how a service would be decommissioned at the business case stage, what customers would lose and what would happen to the data. Teams can write end scenarios, track who uses each part of a system from the outset, and remove features regularly to stay agile. Organisations should also build a closing capability, a team with experience, sponsorship and a process, since the speaker's own teams had none when retiring large services.

talks.title: Scot-Secure Summit 2023 Edinburgh
talks.teaser: Coverage of Scot-Secure Summit 2023 Edinburgh from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session from the Scot-Secure Summit 2023 in Edinburgh features three focused presentations followed by a panel Q&A session moderated by Mark Stephen. The presentations address three distinct aspects of information security: democratizing security through internal training workshops, architecting privacy-enhancing technologies under regulatory pressure, and communicating effectively with executive board members. The session concludes with audience discussions exploring legal implications of privacy, retention of cybersecurity talent, and improving gender diversity in tech.

### Key Topics
- **Engaging Non-Security Teams with Workshops:** Gwen Diagram, Head of Engineering at Glean, shares strategies for running engaging internal security workshops. Drawing from her background as a tester and engineering leader, she demonstrates how to use tools like OWASP Juice Shop, incident response war games, the Elevation of Privilege card game, OWASP ZAP, threat modeling with STRIDE and personas, and intentionally vulnerable application builds to cultivate security awareness across engineering and IT.
- **Application Security via Anonymization (Anonymous Mode):** Leo Cunningham (CISO) and Caius Shashtokush (Application Security Engineer) from Flo Health discuss developing "Anonymous Mode" for their health and period-tracking app. Spurred by the overturning of Roe v. Wade in the US and geopolitical events affecting their workforce, Flo partnered with Cloudflare to implement Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) and binary HTTP to decouple reproductive health data from personally identifiable information (PII).
- **Board-Level Security Communication:** Lena Smart, CISO at MongoDB, provides guidance on briefing corporate boards of directors. She highlights the importance of understanding the board’s core concerns, preparing five-sentence elevator pitches, adopting structured briefing formats (such as the AWS memo format), avoiding technical jargon, and never fabricating answers under pressure.
- **Panel Discussion and Q&A:** The speakers address audience inquiries regarding potential legal challenges against anonymized data, maintaining private bug bounty programs, scaling training programs, retaining security talent through continuous learning and internal security champions programs, and addressing gender disparities in cybersecurity.

### Technical Details
- **Workshop Tooling and Frameworks:** Juice Shop serves as a self-contained, self-healing capture-the-flag (CTF) and training platform covering the OWASP Top 10. Threat modeling implementations leverage the STRIDE model (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege) expanded with Privacy (gdpr considerations) and Adam Shostack's attacker personas. The Elevation of Privilege card game (played like Hearts) requires agile threat record cards for structured scoring.
- **Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) Architecture:** Flo Health's Anonymous Mode encrypts requests from the client device using public keys and routes traffic through a Cloudflare relay service. Cloudflare strips client IP addresses before forwarding binary HTTP requests to Flo’s application gateway, preventing Flo from correlating incoming health data with user network identifiers. Device-side security measures include segregating client storage and storing access codes in the iOS Keychain.
- **Continuous Security and AppSec Testing:** During rapid development, internal AppSec collaborated in real time via dedicated chat channels with external penetration testers. Post-launch security relies on a private bug bounty program, threat modeling for bot mitigation (transitioning from IP-based blocking to web application firewalls and API structure analysis), and plans to open-source client-side encryption logic.
- **Executive Reporting Mechanisms:** MongoDb utilizes a dedicated one-hour quarterly board session focused purely on security. Presentations rely on pre-circulated 10–15 page AWS-style memos featuring an executive statement of intent, an agenda, and detailed technical addenda rather than cluttered slide decks.

### Takeaways
- **Engage Broadly Across the Organization:** Developers, IT staff, and compliance personnel are eager to learn security when offered gamified, hands-on, and relevant training rather than passive lectures.
- **Decouple Data to Enforce Privacy:** When regulatory or external threats risk user data exposure, architectural solutions like Oblivious HTTP can mathematically and operationally ensure sensitive user records cannot be linked to individual identities.
- **Communicate as an Authentic Expert:** Interacting with corporate boards requires brevity, rigorous preparation, calm transparency when information is unavailable, and framing technical risk around core business assets.

talks.title: ITSX Summit 2023 Edinburgh
talks.teaser: Three IT leaders show how better ServiceNow UX, asset housekeeping, and fewer platform emails cut waste, cost, and carbon.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a UX-focused view of enterprise service portals built on ServiceNow. A nursery-rhyme metaphor illustrates how wrong assumptions distort design: user research and personas (loaders, new starters, approvers, senior management) should drive layout, terminology, accessibility, and mobile-first flows instead of cramming content above the fold, stacking guided tours, or labeling simple requests as major incidents.

A second segment frames tech waste across hardware, software, and cloud. Physical kit and peripherals pile up; disposal and data-leak risk can be severe. Software hoarding drives license cost and upgrade debt. Cloud spend accrues every second idle instances run, so usage data must become timely decisions, with centralized sourcing for spot, reserved, and flexible contracts aligned to actual consumption.

The closing presentation quantifies automated ServiceNow email at scale—millions per year and tens of tons of CO2—and describes shifting notifications to Teams, mobile queues, and dashboards. Targeted eliminations cut daily volume sharply while preserving audit needs where email still matters. Q&A extends the thread to notification carbon, governance versus action, trust, and whether leaner interfaces carry a design obligation on carbon intensity.

talks.title: Expo22 - Keynote
talks.teaser: Panellists discuss the scale of women's underrepresentation in Scotland's tech sector and what employers can do about it.
talks.summary:
This panel asked why women remain underrepresented in Scotland's technology sector and whether progress is real. Panellists noted that statistics vary between UK, European and Scottish sources, and that organisations can gather data without acting on it. Women were described as a small share of technology students and jobs, with representation falling at senior levels.

Barriers included unconscious bias, such as questions women founders get about family and childcare that men rarely hear, and women-led firms being dismissed as lifestyle businesses. Hybrid working was seen as double-edged, since fewer women attend the office and miss informal conversations that shape promotion. Girls' interest was said to drop between ages 10 and 14, when subject choices separate them from peers. Only one to two percent of venture funding was said to reach women, with less for women of colour.

Suggested actions included making inclusive recruitment routine, trusting staff with flexible hours, and swapping the gender in a question to test for bias. Men were urged to speak up when women are interrupted, and equity was preferred to equality. The takeaway was to measure progress, share practices that work, and remember that inclusion is what keeps diverse hires in post.

talks.title: Expo22 - Keynote
talks.teaser: Panelists explore Scotland's digital skills gap, covering school pathways, apprenticeships, retraining and keeping talent.
talks.summary:
The session frames Scotland's digital skills gap with figures: the tech sector adds about 7.5 billion pounds to the economy and employs around 100,000 people, yet employers struggle to fill record numbers of vacancies. The moderator introduces four panelists, including a computing science teacher, a retraining organisation's delivery lead, a company founder and chief executive, and a manager from a national skills agency.

Much of the discussion covers perception and pipelines. One panelist argues that people misunderstand the industry, which involves product design, analysis and testing as much as coding, and notes how few girls apply for apprenticeships. The computing teacher describes parents and teachers who lack awareness, a subject missing from some secondary schools, and proposes making computing a core subject taught until third year. Retraining career changers, a short pre-apprenticeship course and businesses reskilling existing staff are offered as ways to widen the pool, while the agency points to a shrinking working-age population and reduced migration as structural pressures.

Later the panel turns to retention and role models. Panelists say training and visible progression keep staff, apprentices tend to stay longer, and industry visits to classrooms help challenge assumptions. In a closing billboard exercise, suggestions included naming the subject computing science, showing salaries and career paths, and stressing freedom. The takeaway is that closing the gap depends on awareness, school-to-work pathways and keeping the people already in the workforce.

talks.title: Expo 2022 - Chris Yule
talks.teaser: Traces how ransomware gangs operate, from initial access to encryption, and why early detection and response matter.
talks.summary:
Chris Yule uses ransomware as the main example of the threat landscape, since it drives most of the incident response work at Secureworks. He opens with a 2021 case at a US travel services firm, where a phishing document led to a loader, a reverse shell, credential dumping and reconnaissance. Over about seven days the intruders stole data and then ran encryption from a domain controller, typically at night or at weekends.

The middle of the talk covers who is behind these attacks. An Iranian state-linked group was seen running ransomware campaigns against Western targets, and an operational security mistake in a ransom note's metadata helped the team identify two individuals later charged in the US. Leaked Conti chat logs let the team link several ransomware families and a Russian crime group, and Yule argues the threat is human, not just technical. He also describes initial access trends: stolen credentials and commodity loaders remain common, while exploitation of internet-facing devices has grown, with scanning starting within hours of a public exploit.

Paying a ransom does not guarantee quick recovery, since decryptors can be unreliable and gangs may return. He stresses incident response planning, patching public-facing systems within hours, and writing specific detections for tools such as Cobalt Strike. In a 2022 case, a Sunday detection of Conti-linked reconnaissance led to 79 compromised hosts being identified and the intruder evicted in about 36 hours.

talks.title: al Transformation Summit 2022 Session 2: C
talks.teaser: Shows how camera passenger counts and machine learning can help cities tune public transport schedules and fleet use.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that cities should start from local context when tackling public transport problems, rather than fitting off-the-shelf software to them. The speaker contrasts fast-moving future mobility, such as autonomous vehicles and shared scooters, with public transit, which is still run like an industrial enterprise. Funding gaps, many stakeholders, and the daily balance between operating cost, environmental impact and passenger comfort slow change.

The technical part describes a data platform built mostly from open-source components: Kafka for event streams, Kubernetes and Rancher for deployment, Jenkins pipelines, and kubeflow to serve machine learning models behind load balancing. In Sofia, cameras on buses, trams and trolleys feed snapshots into a model, trained on 50,000 snapshots, that counts passengers across the network without special hardware. Counts are combined with anonymised mobile operator data, origin-destination heat maps, and efficiency indexes for lines that factor in waiting time, delays and crowding. One example cut a bus line's journey from 53 to 42 minutes, and a schedule optimisation reduced the number of courses threefold while keeping average crowding between 1 and 1.2 passengers per seat.

The closing section makes the point that operators, unions and procurement teams resisted reorganisation, so behavioural factors have to be understood and worked around. The practical takeaways are to begin with local context, use accessible open tools, prototype quickly, and scale only the approaches that work.

talks.title: al Transformation Summit 2022 Session 2: F
talks.teaser: Argues data is often neglected in digital transformation and offers iterative, business-focused examples that keep projects on track.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that data is often the missing piece in digital transformation programs. The speaker, who works for a data software company, says budgets tend to go to apps and front ends while data work gets a small share, and that projects stall when data is treated as a cleanup task just before launch. One example is a used-car pricing app that recommended dealers stock one budget model because of its wholesale-to-retail margin. Another is a vehicle lookup tool that had to answer within three seconds, where the team checked a few executives' cars by hand before launch.

The middle of the talk looks at why teams do not connect. A data cleanse done once before launch breaks as soon as the underlying process changes. Reporting teams already solve the same reconciliation problems every day but are not involved in the transformation, and the same stakeholders fund both groups without coordinating them. Several examples show a different approach. An aerospace engine team used lightweight screening models to reject weak blade designs before running heavy fluid dynamics simulations, which cut iteration time. A manufacturing quality engineer shortened the time needed to detect production issues by applying familiar techniques to data with a small tool. A recruitment service routed job applications to the right queue by country.

The closing point is that transformation should be iterative and less grandiose, building skills in existing staff and joining data and digital teams together. The speaker also warns against discarding the new detail that transformed processes generate just to match an old report format.

talks.title: al Transformation Summit 2022 Session 2: G
talks.teaser: Explains SASE, the cloud-delivered networking and security model, and walks through a recorded product demo.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the idea behind SASE, a term Gartner introduced in 2019 for combining cloud networking and cloud security into one subscription. The speaker explains that the pandemic pushed many organisations to move online quickly, often leaving networking and security as an afterthought. He gives an example of a cloud contract signed before the network provider had interconnects ready, which delayed the move by nine months. He also argues that observability is a third pillar, since traditional data centre tools cannot show where a slow connection problem lies.

A colleague then walks through a pre-recorded video of the unified offering, as a live demo was avoided. The first step onboards branch sites by assigning Meraki-equipped offices to US or EU cloud hubs, and the next pulls users and groups from an existing directory. Remote users are placed in regional access points and checked against an endpoint posture profile that denies anything not on the approved list, such as particular operating systems and browsers. The final part applies policy to SaaS applications by category, blocking a group of gambling sites with one rule, and to private applications, which are grouped and reached through a browser without a VPN. A demonstration shows a user who is not a doctor being denied a medical portal after multi-factor sign-in.

The closing takeaways for a digital transformation plan are to set networking and security architecture principles before signing cloud contracts, build them into the operating model, and check whether existing partners have networking and security skills. The product was presented as version 1.0, currently covering the US and EU.

talks.title: al Transformation Summit 2022 Session 1
talks.teaser: al Transformation Summit 2022 Session 1.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Chaired by Mark Steven, this opening session of the 8th Annual Digital Transformation Summit brings together three distinct perspectives on digital transformation, technology adoption, and organizational impact. The presentations and subsequent panel Q&A focus on keeping human needs at the center of change, overcoming operational hurdles in data science, and leveraging open satellite earth observation data for environmental and business intelligence.

### Key Topics

#### Human-Centric Transformation and Tech for Good
Graham Johnson (CEO of Retail and Distribution at The Donaldson Group) argues that digital transformation should fundamentally serve people rather than technology for its own sake. Drawing on his experience, he outlines core transformation lessons: treating programs as continuous evolution rather than rigid, one-off changes; avoiding isolated "VIP clubs" of top talent that pull domain experts away from day-to-day realities; winning "hearts and minds" instead of imposing unrealistic timelines; and focusing on what new tools enable for colleagues and customers rather than simply what systems they replace. Highlighting digital inequality—where only 44% of a representative 100-person global village has internet access—he calls for an "Industry 6.0" centered on humans and social equity. He details the evolution of the Scottish Tech Army into the Tech for Good Alliance, an initiative addressing social justice, digital inclusion, skills development, and climate sustainability by mobilizing skilled tech volunteers for the third sector.

#### Practical Realities of Data Science and MLOps
Leanne Fitzpatrick (Director of Data Science at the Financial Times) discusses the organizational realities of delivering impact through data science, machine learning, and AI. She warns against unrealistic expectations where organizations assume models immediately create business value without solid data infrastructure. Impact requires balancing technical execution (dependency management, scaling, Version Control, observability, and MLOps pipelines) with an open team culture (trust, curiosity, peer review) and organizational embedding. Fitzpatrick highlights the challenge of calculating return on investment (ROI) in ML, advocating that teams map technical metrics (such as NLP accuracy or maximum likelihood estimation) directly to core business KPIs like engagement and bottom-line revenue. She also emphasizes deprecating obsolete projects and fostering cross-functional skills such as change management and data governance.

#### Satellite Data, Earth Observation, and Natural Capital
Professor Edward Mitchard (Co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer at Space Intelligence) examines the vast, underutilized repository of free satellite data provided by agencies such as the European Space Agency (ESA). He details three core remote sensing modalities: Optical satellite imagery (e.g., Sentinel-2), which captures spectral bands but is impeded by night and persistent cloud cover; Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR, e.g., Sentinel-1), which penetrates clouds and night to measure surface roughness, moisture, and forest biomass; and spaceborne LiDAR (e.g., NASA's GEDI on the International Space Station), which provides precise tree height measurements along orbital tracks. Combining these datasets with machine learning enables continuous mapping of forest biomass, carbon sequestration, and land-cover change. Mitchard explains how this intelligence underpins nature-based carbon credits, Scottish Government natural capital accounting (such as the Natural Capital Asset Index), regulatory compliance (e.g., zero deforestation, Biodiversity Net Gain), and verifiable ESG metrics.

### Technical Details
- **Remote Sensing and AI Pipelines**: Space Intelligence processes terabytes of multi-sensor data in AWS and GCP. Optical (10 m resolution Sentinel-2), SAR microwave backscatter (Sentinel-1), and LiDAR photon arrival timings (GEDI 25 m footprints) are cleaned, aligned, and merged using machine learning models to interpolate biomass maps and produce land-cover classifications (including 22 distinct Scottish land categories).
- **Data Architecture Foundations**: Successful ML requires an underlying hierarchy: structured data platforms and pipelines (data engineers), business intelligence/reporting, analytics, and finally predictive/prescriptive data science and MLOps at the apex.

### Takeaways
Successful digital transformation relies on robust technical foundations, cultural alignment, and user-focused outcomes. Whether mobilizing skilled volunteers for charities, connecting ML models to operational decisions, or turning satellite feeds into environmental dashboards, technology acts as an enabler rather than an end in itself.

talks.title: al Transformation Summit 2022 Session 2: A
talks.teaser: Makes the case for setting data strategy before choosing digital tools, with advice on data quality, KPIs and senior buy-in.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many organisations pick data tools in an ad hoc way, with each department signing up for its own product. The result is disconnected, sometimes duplicated data that nobody can easily combine. The speaker says this blocks useful reporting and AI projects, and that senior managers often cannot see current figures without waiting for a report. Tool decisions tend to be made without the right people in the room, and data is treated as an afterthought until choices are already made.

The middle of the talk proposes starting with business goals and the questions each team wants answered, then building a data strategy and roadmap before selecting software. A worked example involved a client who tracked new customers as a single figure, 37 over a period, with no history or target to compare it against. Planning for AI means thinking early about the data volumes, history and structure it will need, because gaps are hard to fix later. Staff who understand the data they create, and a named owner for each data set, matter as much as the technology.

In the closing questions, the speaker described mapping existing data by interviewing people across the company and building simple data maps and dictionaries. Synthetic data and external sources such as weather were mentioned as ways to bridge gaps when historical records are missing. The main takeaways are to involve senior management early, upskill existing teams, and ask what the business needs to know before committing to any digital tool.

talks.title: Fintech Summit 2022 Edinburgh
talks.teaser: Surveys how fintech firms can build resilience, improve financial health and time payment collections amid rising living costs.
talks.summary:
The opening session of a Scottish fintech summit looked at how the sector has changed since 2007, when the first iPhone launched and the collapse of Northern Rock sparked a bank run. Starling Bank's chief technology advocate, Jason mod, argued that fintech has to meet both the demand for change and the need for resilience, and that customer financial data belongs to the customer. He described building systems that check and recheck their own instructions, and he named three resilience challenges: legacy technology, payment chains that span many organisations, and sustainable business models.

Caroline Murphy, managing director at Moneybox, turned to financial resilience in the UK. She cited research showing that average household savings covered about 24 days in 2020, falling to 19 days, and said a third of households in 2014 could not last a week. She linked this to weak financial education, the shift from defined benefit to defined contribution pensions, and the role of pension search tools, automated savings and clearer dashboards in helping people plan.

Marika Lomas, head of payments at Cleo, explained how rising costs, more frequent card freezes and easier disputes make recurring payments harder to collect. Using data on when customers are paid, her team moved collection attempts to match income timing, which she said improved payment success by nearly 30 percent and reduced cancellations by six percent. She argued that waiting to collect helps customers avoid overdraft fees and helps the business keep its revenue.

talks.teaser: Coverage of North 2022 from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Susan Kruger presents the PICTURES program of work, managed for the University of Dundee's Health Informatics Centre in collaboration with Public Health Scotland, the University of Edinburgh, Abertay, and industry partner Aridhia. Funded by a Medical Research Council grant, the project expands the capabilities of safe havens and trusted research environments (TREs) in Scotland to handle large-scale, routinely collected medical imaging data (specifically DICOM radiology files) for AI training and healthcare research while safeguarding patient confidentiality. The core outcome is the live Scottish Medical Imaging (SMI) service hosted within Scotland's National Safe Haven.

### Key Topics
- **Medical Imaging Challenges**: In Scotland, over 3.5 million radiological examinations occur annually, generating massive quantities of unstructured DICOM data stored in the national PACS archive. While invaluable for training clinical AI models (e.g., detecting early signs of lung cancer, emphysema, or cardiovascular conditions), the data is unstructured, inconsistently labeled, complex, and filled with personally identifiable information (PII).
- **The Five Safes Framework**: The infrastructure operates under the five safes model established in Scottish safe havens: safe people (accredited researchers), safe projects (governance ensuring ethical public benefit), safe settings (secure environments), safe data (de-identified minimal data), and safe outputs (statistical disclosure control prior to export).
- **Governance and Legal Framework**: In Scotland, secondary use of pseudonymized healthcare data is legally permitted when public benefit is demonstrated and patient privacy is protected. Governance involves local Caldicott groups across 14 NHS health boards as well as the national Public Benefit and Privacy Panel (PBPP).

### Technical Details
- **Data Ingestion and Scale**: In 2018, partner eDRIS (part of Public Health Scotland) obtained a research copy of over 1.5 petabytes of national PACS data spanning 2010 to 2018.
- **Architecture and Security Zones**: SMI employs a microservices-based architecture conceptually divided into three audited zones: a restricted Red Zone housing raw identifiable data with automated processing, de-identified intermediate zones, and an analytic Green Zone. In the Green Zone, high-risk research is isolated inside Private Project Spaces (PPS) with automated software provisioning using Ansible playbooks (e.g., TensorFlow).
- **De-identification and Redaction**: Patient identifiers reside in DICOM header tags, structured report text, and embedded image pixels. Initial releases use omission (single-layer primary images with minimal PII risk), while ongoing work employs tools like the Clinical Trials Processor (CTP) to redact specific pixel coordinates. Willful re-identification remains an offence.
- **Cohort Building Tools**: To extract research-specific image IDs, the platform uses the Research Data Management Platform (RDMP) for cataloging, versioning, and querying DICOM metadata; SemEHR (Semantic Electronic Health Record) natural language processing for free-text structured reports; and autoencoders for unsupervised image representation, feature extraction, and similarity-based image retrieval.

### Takeaways
The live SMI service enables population-scale, real-world imaging data to be safely interrogated for clinical AI development without compromising patient privacy. By automating extraction, standardization, and de-identification within a governed safe haven, the PICTURES platform facilitates reproducible medical research and helps alleviate radiologist workload.

talks.title: Cloud First 2021 - Session 2: Breakout Sessions
talks.teaser: Three cloud sessions cover healthcare analytics, GDPR duties for cloud providers, and compliance monitoring across hybrid estates.
talks.summary:
The recording covers three breakout talks. Jonathan Forbes, from a digital pharmacy, describes running operations and analytics on cloud platforms, with infrastructure defined as code and a layered analytics design. He shows demand trends and drug price data, then asks whether information gathered during recent disruption still holds value for forecasting.

Laura Irvin, a data protection lawyer, explains the duties of cloud service providers as processors under the GDPR. Providers need written contracts, must act only on the customer's instructions, and must manage sub-processors. She describes security as a risk-based obligation and reviews the post-Brexit position on transfers, including the loss of the Privacy Shield arrangement for US transfers, which leaves organisations needing extra safeguards and contract clauses.

Mark Mitchell, a security engineering manager, argues that compliance has to be continuous across on-premises and public cloud estates. He covers posture management that checks builds against policy and automatic remediation, and warns that full logging produces huge volumes that make manual threat hunting impractical. He closes with a case of an exposed cloud storage bucket holding sensitive government records, and advice on account governance such as centralised logins, multifactor authentication and billing monitoring.

talks.title: Leader Summit 2021 | Session 1
talks.teaser: Three speakers examine how remote work, burnout and disruption are reshaping leadership, and what managers can do about it.
talks.summary:
The opening session of the digital leader summit looked at how the pandemic has changed work. Abigail Martz, a professor of the future of work, presented findings from a research project that interviewed 80 UK workers four times and surveyed about 1,400 home workers. She argued that the sudden move to homeworking was a rushed experiment and not a reliable guide to the future. Her findings covered uneven home office space, crowded households, and inadequate equipment, with over half of people reporting musculoskeletal problems. She also questioned a reported productivity rise of over 30 percent, suggesting it reflected longer hours, fewer breaks and heavy video call schedules.

Bianca Best, managing director of a digital transformation consultancy, framed remote work as a hidden burnout crisis. She linked excessive productivity to chronic stress and argued that back-to-back meetings with no gaps were unsustainable. Her suggested responses included prioritising work each week, shortening default meeting lengths, requiring clear agendas, and protecting boundaries between work and home. John Abel, a technical director in the office of the CTO at Google, argued that disruption creates opportunity when organisations focus on culture, remove friction, clarify what they are known for, and make room for reflection and diverse thinking.

The question and answer period covered mental health at work, measuring productivity by outcomes rather than hours, and the risk of a two-tier hybrid workforce. The speakers agreed that leaders should be open about their own struggles, and that decisions about hybrid working would need to be tested and revised over time.

talks.title: Leader Summit 2021 | Session 2
talks.teaser: Leaders weigh culture, roadmaps and shifting consumer behaviour after a year of remote work and pandemic disruption.
talks.summary:
This breakout session from the DIGIT Leader Summit 2021 featured three business speakers on how organisations are adapting after a year of remote working. Alistair Rennie, chief technical officer, described how home working has blurred boundaries, weakened team bonding and strained motivation. To onboard seven new staff, he replaced a short office tour with a half-day structured induction, added daily stand-ups and regular one-to-ones, and spread leadership responsibility through his team structure. He reported a productivity rise of 15-20 percent alongside a warning not to push people too far.

Duane Pascal argued that agile roadmaps work best as a shared visual tool that connects business outcomes to delivery work, rather than a fixed list of features. He recommended tracking outcomes over outputs and turning uncertainty into discovery actions. Each initiative would be scored for confidence against four risks: value, usability, feasibility and viability. Research such as surveys, usability tests or prototypes would then be planned to raise confidence before building.

Elena Vedli presented five consumer behaviour shifts linked to the pandemic: purpose-driven buying, a focus on health, demand for hygiene and contactless options, a preference for convenience, and seamless movement between physical and digital shopping. Her advice was to remove friction from customer journeys and to show genuine values, since she warned that greenwashing is quickly spotted and not forgiven. Together the talks pointed leaders to keep culture, planning and customer experience under regular review.

talks.title: Data Protection Summit 10 Dec Session 3
talks.teaser: Panelists explain lawful bases for sensitive data, data localization and post-Schrems II transfer rules.
talks.summary:
Toby Hayes, a data protection controller, argues that organisations often wrongly assume explicit consent is needed for sensitive processing. He explains that special category data needs both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9 condition, plus an appropriate policy document under the UK Data Protection Act 2018. The scenarios cover gender pay reporting, ethnicity monitoring for equality, COVID-19 absence records and temperature screening, where collecting no data at all may be the simplest route.

Vivian explains data localisation, which requires data to stay in its country of origin, and contrasts it with data sovereignty. She lists drivers such as regulators wanting fast access, uneven security standards and concerns for local businesses. She covers forms including equivalence rules, consent restrictions, local copy rules and outsourcing limits, and warns that localisation adds cost and fragments customer views in financial services. She recommends principle-based mutual recognition, rules on access rather than storage location, and trade agreements.

Caitlin Fennessy looks at the Schrems II ruling, which invalidated Privacy Shield but upheld standard contractual clauses that require case-by-case assessments. She describes how firms adopted transfer impact assessments and additional safeguards, and how draft EDPB guidance leaned on encryption while raising concerns for cloud and general business processing. She argues that localisation may not solve surveillance concerns and calls for multilateral cooperation on binding principles.

talks.title: FinTech Summit 29/09/20 Session 4
talks.teaser: Panellists weigh open banking's uptake, consumer trust and consent, and its growth in lending and payments.
talks.summary:
This panel from a fintech summit reviews how open banking has developed, covering uptake, its effect on consumers, and remaining challenges around trust and transparency. Panellists say most people need not know the term, and cite UK figures of up to about 160,000 monthly users. Credit assessment is offered as a clear consumer benefit, since recent bank transaction history gives lenders a more current picture than traditional credit files.

Attention then moves to consent and data protection. The speakers stress explicit, active consent that states who receives which data and from which account, and plain-language explanations over long privacy policies. On the corporate side, batch-based reconciliation is described as a barrier to real-time payments, while lower fees and faster certainty are cited as benefits.

Closing remarks touch on the pandemic accelerating digital change and on certificate revocation linked to the end of the Brexit transition period, which the panel expects the industry to resolve. Looking ahead, the panel sees common open banking standards as a route to data sharing across other sectors, with consumers in control of their own data.

talks.title: MarTech Summit 24/02/21 Session 1
talks.teaser: Traces how marketing moved to digital channels and data-driven insight, then debates tracking and trust with a panel.

Peter Proud opened by tracing how marketing and IT began working together. He recounted a 2006 meeting with Unilever's marketing teams on the connected consumer, a Dove campaign on MSN that collected 180,000 survey responses in three days, and a Microsoft initiative that led to a cloud-based stack for fast, large-scale digital delivery. He argued that customers now move between channels, so the right information has to arrive quickly and reliably.

Vivian McLaren, head of marketing at idea gen, argued that many organisations still use digital marketing poorly, citing a 2020 finding that 49 of the FTSE 100 were missing search opportunities. She explained how cancelled events during lockdown pushed her firm toward search, paid channels, LinkedIn and persona-based content, with results tracked through marketing qualified leads in Pardot and Salesforce. Christine Bailey then covered customer insight, segmentation, content planning and lead generation, warning against following data blindly and against attribution errors that serve the wrong ads.

The closing panel discussed tracking, cookies and privacy. Speakers agreed that shoppers expect relevant offers but disagreed on how willingly people give up their data. They pointed to GDPR as a turning point and noted that few users read privacy policies. The main takeaway was that marketers should use data to deliver relevance, stay transparent about collection and question what their models tell them.

talks.title: 's Digital Transformation 2020 Virtual Summit Session 4
talks.teaser: Speakers explore how sustainability strategy, energy grid digital upgrades and waste tracking shape business decisions.
talks.summary:
This closing session of a virtual digital transformation event featured three speakers on how businesses are responding to growing public expectations around sustainability, trust and ethics. Betsy Reed framed sustainability as covering social impact as well as environmental issues. She argued that a strategy needs leadership and buy-in at every level, early involvement from communications staff, and performance measures that go beyond carbon and energy to include stakeholder engagement and trust.

Ian Dugan, who leads IT at SSE, described how its transmission business is using digital transformation to support a net zero electricity grid. He explained that renewable power from the north of Scotland must be moved to population centres further south, with a planned investment of 2.4 billion pounds over five years and a 50 million pound digital programme. He also covered a regulator requirement for a digital strategy, consolidating asset data into a single source of truth, and using drone imagery to reduce staff exposure to dangerous sites.

Michael Groves argued that waste is difficult to measure and manage, and that making material flows visible is the first step toward treating it as a resource. He described a platform that combines waste-sector knowledge with software and data science, and mentioned a UK plan for digital waste tracking. The panel then discussed producer responsibility, data storage footprints, and whether sustainability momentum would survive a recession, with the shared view that transparency and measurable results build lasting trust.

talks.title: Fintech Summit 2020 Fortinet Breakout |D
talks.teaser: Surveys how digital innovation is reshaping cyber risk for financial services, with a vendor's view on network and cloud defenses.
talks.summary:
This vendor-led session looks at how financial services organisations are changing and why cyber risk grows along with digital innovation. The speaker contrasts emerging fintech firms, which focus on the customer, with traditional banks that must transform while keeping risk at an acceptable level. Risk is framed as a question of how much is acceptable rather than something good or bad. Threats are described as coming mainly from organised cybercriminals, along with insiders, partners and some foreign states, with financial motives and data, intellectual property and service disruption as the main targets.

The middle of the talk covers consequences of attacks, such as business disruption and information loss, and names a lack of qualified staff as a core problem. Advice centres on visibility, a structured approach to security, simpler compliance, and combining technology with process and people. The speaker then walks through network and cloud topics: zero trust network access, SD-WAN and SD-branch for simpler branch management, segmentation that looks beyond north-south traffic, hybrid cloud adoption and the shared responsibility model in public cloud, and network access control for IoT and OT devices.

The closing section presents AI as a way to help predict and prevent threats, correlate insider activity and automate responses to relieve pressure on staff. The speaker stresses that there is no single fix. The session ended with a short question period in which no questions came through, and attendees were pointed to the vendor's exhibitor booth for follow-up.

talks.title: Intelligent Automation 2020 -Runecast Breakout A
talks.teaser: Explains turning scattered vendor knowledge into machine-readable rules that find hidden risks in VMware environments.
talks.summary:
Stan Markov, co-founder and CEO of Runecast, opens with the daily pressures of virtualization operations: outages with hidden causes, constant tracking of best practices and known issues, and manual health and compliance checks during audits. A customer incident, where VMware High Availability failed to restart virtual machines, was traced to a little-known knowledge base article, and checking hundreds of customers for the same problem took weeks.

He notes that over 90 percent of the root causes he reviewed were already published in unstructured sources such as vendor knowledge bases, blogs, compatibility lists and compliance standards. The proposed pipeline crawls these sources, parses and cleans them, extracts entities and noun phrases, translates them into configuration settings and scores confidence, with human administrators validating the resulting rules. A rules engine then matches those rules against an object graph of hosts, virtual machines, datastores and networks, returning groups of objects with risky configurations, and he claims it scales to millions of objects and thousands of rules.

The product, Runecast Analyzer, ships as a single downloadable virtual appliance that connects to vCenter, NSX, Horizon and AWS without agents, and it can run offline with update packages. It also offers an upgrade simulator, historical analysis and compliance reporting. The main takeaway is finding hidden risks before they cause outages while staying audit ready.

talks.title: Intelligent Automation Session 2
talks.teaser: Covers 5G factory automation and machine learning on satellite imagery, with case studies in industry and climate monitoring.
talks.summary:
Steve Evans, chief technical officer for Nokia's global enterprise business in the UK and Ireland, opens with the economic case for Industry 4.0. He argues that physical industries trail digital ones in investment, and that the real bottleneck is moving sensor data to intelligence and back to machines in real time, which low-latency radio networks can address.

He illustrates this with three cases: a port where cameras, drones and asset tracking cut theft and insurance claims; a Nokia factory in Finland where robots and tools are controlled over 5G; and remote monitoring of household power use that lets carers visit older people only when needed. On UK policy, he says Ofcom's release of spectrum lets enterprises build private 5G networks, while city data systems remain siloed. He expects release 16, with true ultra-reliable low-latency 5G, to reach products around the end of the year.

Ed Mitchard, of Space Intelligence, then turns to satellite Earth observation. Thousands of satellites now produce large volumes of mostly free data, and optical and radar sensors capture different things. Machine learning can sharpen imagery, remove clouds and classify land cover. One Scottish land-cover project reached 94 percent accuracy across about 20 classes using carefully checked training data. A Mozambique case checked whether planted trees survived a cyclone, using very high-resolution imagery and a shadow-based tree detector. He closes by stressing that clean ground data matters as much as the algorithm.

talks.title: Intelligent Automation 2020
talks.teaser: Surveys how AI, computer vision and IoT are being applied in factories, warehouses, vertical farms and smart cities.
talks.summary:
This live virtual session on intelligent automation opens with Sarah Mannion of NVIDIA, who contrasts fixed robotic arms that only run programmed tasks with machinery that senses its surroundings and adapts. She outlines three growth areas: predictive production lines using computer vision, smart maintenance that anticipates faults, and smart logistics. Her main case is Ocado, whose warehouse vision system was trained on more than 50,000 line items so it could tell similar products apart and avoid wrong picks and damaged stock. She also describes autonomous warehouse robots at BMW, which make decisions on embedded GPUs while training runs in a data centre.

An agritech company founded by a farmer then describes indoor vertical farming, where automation, IoT sensors and machine learning control climate across stacked growing trays. Its intelligent grid replaces cables so sensors, cameras and lights can hang from one structure, and low-voltage three-phase power avoids LED flicker. The workflow repeats a loop: apply a weather recipe, measure crop and machine responses, then refine the next recipe with machine learning. Growers can also shift energy use against electricity prices.

The final talk covers AI and IoT in smart cities, arguing that energy, water, transport and waste systems must share an integration layer so their data can be combined. Examples include solar-powered trees that provide free energy and environmental readings, smart bins that show residents their recycling, and a canal flood sensor network run by the people who own the devices. The speaker warns that unbalanced training data produces bias and closes with principles of ethical, secure, privacy-preserving and distributed design. In questions, speakers stressed keeping humans involved alongside robots and processing time-critical decisions at the edge.

talks.title: Fintech in Scotland
talks.teaser: Industry voices discuss how financial services are shifting and how Scotland's fintech ecosystem is growing through collaboration.
talks.summary:
This recording from a fintech event in Edinburgh gathers short remarks from industry figures on how financial services are changing. The chair opens by pointing to new regulation that lets challengers enter banking and payments, and to customers who now expect to manage their own money through newer services. The speakers describe a shift from start-ups trying to displace established firms toward partnerships, and they note that the hardest task is bringing new technology into large, long-established organisations.

Several contributors turn to Scotland's ecosystem. They point to strong universities, courses and talent, and say the local scene has gained momentum and can help organisations with good people and ideas scale quickly. Pathways into fintech are a focus, and the sector is described as lively, with growing awareness among institutions.

The closing remarks call the event a possible first step toward a larger global fintech hub in Scotland. For a practitioner, the main takeaway is that a regional ecosystem, collaboration between incumbents and newcomers, and a clear focus on customer value all shape how fintech develops.
